newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds sink, long end suffers most.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds sink, long end suffers most.

text.p: Irish government bonds fell backwards on Thursday with the longer end of the market suffering most of the damage as weak foreign markets and a dearth of buyers took their toll, dealer said.
"The long end of the market in particular has traded away quite badly this afternoon," one dealer said. "There aren't huge flows behind it but prices have been marked down."

Dealers said weaker U.S. Treasuries and German Bunds had been partly to blame for the fall in Irish bond prices, although Ireland was underperforming most other markets thanks to a lack of bid interest.
"There just don't seem to be people in supporting the market, there are no bids for long maturities out there," one said.
By 1610 GMT the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was 35p weaker at 102.00 to yield 5.92 percent while the eight percent bond due 2006 had tumbled 85p to 109.30 to yield 6.56 percent.

Dealers said the market was awaiting Irish end-October credit growth statistics, due from the central bank at 1630 GMT, but analysts said the market's weakness was not caused by pessimism about the numbers.

"The figures would impinge more on the short end than the long end so fears about the figures would cause curve flattening, but in fact we've seen curve steepening," said Padhraic Garvey, senior economist at Riada Stockbrokers.
Riada is forecasting credit growth of 13.2 percent year-on-year in October, at the low end of expectations.
"If we're right the market would take the number very well, and even if the number is 13.5 percent I think the market would take it well," Garvey said.
Most Irish economists expect a figure in the range of 13.2 to 14 percent.
